newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Ecuador's new government disappoints oil investors.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's new government disappoints oil investors.

text.p: Foreign oil companies operating in Ecuador privately expressed disappointment at the choice of the country's new energy administration, saying they feared it would be unreceptive to foreign investment and unlikely to extend liberalisation.

Last week, center-left deputy Raul Baca was appointed Ecuador's new energy minister. Ex-energy minister Rafael Almeida is favorite to be the new president of the state oil company PetroEcuador, oil company executives in Ecuador said.

Both officials served in the left-wing government of Rodrigo Borja (1988-1992) and are known to favor government intervention. Also, Baca is close to the trade unions and has been a critic of privatization in the energy sector.

"I don't think they are going to do anything fast that's going to be friendly to foreign investors," said one foreign oil company executive in Ecuador. "These people have a high regard for national industrial capability and don't feel reliant on foreign investment."

After the Bucaram administration, which clashed very publicly last year with Ecuador's biggest foreign oil investor, Maxus, oil executives say the new leaders may have a smoother style. But they expect more delays to a desperately-needed expansion of Ecuador's export capacity.
The delays could mean that existing exploration contracts would lapse without moving to the development phase.

"Ecuador has done itself a disservice first by electing Bucaram and second, in the short term, by getting rid of him," said Rafael Quijano, Latin American analyst for Petroleum Finance Corp in Washington. "It will take some time to regain the confidence of investors in the oil industry, both upstream and downstream."

Just one day into the job, Baca suspended a tender for the construction of a 246,000 barrel per day (bpd) new SOCO pipeline to run alongside an existing 320,000 bpd SOTE line, saying the tender process "lacked transparency". The SOTE pipeline carries about 90 percent of Ecuador's oil output.
Oil executives say the new minister has come out in favour of expanding capacity on the SOTE line by about 50,000 bpd, which they would support.

"We've had a chicken and egg situation for some time," said a foreign oil executive in Ecuador. "A lot of companies like Occidental, Oryx, Maxus and Elf have the ability to do more development work and produce higher volumes of oil, but because the limits of transportation there's no reason to make those investments."

Ecuador's current production of around 360,000 bpd could be lifted by up to 50 percent by two undeveloped projects, oil executives say. One was the Villano field, jointly owned by Atlantic Richfield Co RCO (60 percent) and Agip SpA (40 percent), containing about 160 million barrels in recoverable reserves. The other was PetroEcuador's "Ishpingo, Tambo Cocha, Tiputini" complex with an estimated 700 million barrels in reserves.
One oil company manager said these two fields could produce up to 150,000 bpd of oil.
"If they develop the new field, they will need a new line unless they wait for existing production to decline," he said.

Quijano said the Bucaram administration was "amateurish" in its dealings with the oil industry, but that Bucaram himself was someone who could get things done. "The (Bucaram) administration was able to keep the union out of the policy decisions in the oil industry and that is perhaps the only positive thing we might miss in the new administration," he said.

The left-wing leanings of Ecuador's new oil administration would also be felt in the petroleum retailing sector, Quijano said. "There is substantial interest by many international companies to play a more active role in retailing, but for that you need a marketplace. I think that could be put in jeopardy by the colour of the ministers."

But the marketing of Ecuador's crude exports was not expected to change. One Ecuadorean government source said: "Marketing is a technical matter that has nothing to do with politics." He said about half of Ecuador's exports went to the United States, and other customers included Korea, Chile and other Latin American markets., ((--Caracas newsroom, +582 505 2600))
